title: Vinted OS
subtitle: Smart listing management for Vinted sellers
description: A productivity platform designed to streamline inventory management for Vinted sellers by centralizing listing organization, performance tracking, and workflow automation. The system provides tools for monitoring product metrics, managing large inventories, accelerating listing and relisting processes, and improving operational efficiency. The project demonstrates practical software development, process optimization, data organization, and user-focused interface design for real-world e-commerce applications.
objectives: Centralize inventory and listing data that was previously scattered across the Vinted app and spreadsheets.
Reduce the manual effort of relisting and refreshing stale product listings.
Surface performance metrics (views, likes, sell-through time) to guide pricing and relisting decisions.
outcome: A working personal tool that manages my own Vinted inventory end-to-end. AI-assisted development was used throughout to accelerate iteration and explore automation approaches I hadn't used before, though some workflows are still being validated before I'd call the system fully tested.

story.text: Managing a growing catalogue of second-hand listings on Vinted by hand was slow and error-prone: tracking which items needed relisting, which were underpriced, and which had stopped getting views required constant manual checking with no central view of the inventory.

I looked at how existing sellers organize inventory (spreadsheets, note apps) and identified the recurring pain points: no automation, no historical performance tracking, and no single source of truth for what's listed, sold, or pending.

I designed a simple data model around listings, with fields for status, price history, and engagement metrics, and planned a set of automation hooks (relisting, price adjustment suggestions) that could be layered on top once the core system was stable.

Built primarily in Python, using AI coding assistants to accelerate boilerplate, validate edge cases, and explore automation patterns for interacting with listing data. Development is iterative, with each session adding a well-scoped feature rather than a big-bang rewrite.

The tool now organizes my inventory, tracks basic performance signals, and forms the base for future automation like scheduled relisting. It is in active, ongoing use, though I haven't yet been able to test every workflow end-to-end.

Using AI as a development accelerator works best when I stay the one making architectural decisions. It's fastest for boilerplate and exploration, but the data model and priorities still need deliberate human design.

items.text: Keeping the data model simple enough to maintain solo while still capturing enough history to make useful pricing/relisting suggestions.

items.label: Future Improvements

title: Personal Portfolio
subtitle: Premium engineering portfolio, framework-free
description: A premium engineering portfolio developed using HTML5, CSS3, and Vanilla JavaScript, with a strong emphasis on performance, accessibility, and user experience. The website showcases engineering projects through responsive layouts, smooth animations, and interactive visual elements while maintaining clean architecture and optimized code. The project demonstrates frontend development skills, UI/UX design principles, performance optimization, and the ability to build scalable, framework-free web applications suitable for professional presentation.
objectives: Present my engineering projects with the depth of real case studies, not just a list of links.
Build a fast, accessible, framework-free site that stays easy to extend as new projects are added.
Use AI as a genuine development accelerator while keeping full control over architecture and content.
outcome: A production site with a reusable data-driven project system: every project page assembles itself from a single JSON record, so adding a new case study never requires touching the templates.

story.text: A generic portfolio template doesn't show how I actually think as an engineer. It lists projects instead of explaining the reasoning, trade-offs, and results behind them.

I designed a component system (cards, status pills, highlight badges, filter bar) and a per-project data contract so every project, software or mechanical, renders a consistent, complete case study regardless of its content.

Built with plain HTML5, CSS3, and vanilla JavaScript modules (no framework), with AI assistance used heavily for iteration speed, debugging, and refactors, while I directed the architecture and design decisions.

Iterated on performance (capping canvas pixel density, batching draw calls, removing expensive blur filters) after noticing jank on ambient background effects, and fixed an interaction bug where 3D card tilt made action buttons hard to click.
A fast, accessible site where every project, regardless of discipline, gets a real case study page: overview, my contribution, an engineering story, and links to source/resources.
Treating the portfolio itself as an engineering project, with a real data model and iteration cycle, produced a much more maintainable result than hand-writing each page.

groups.label: Architecture
items: Static HTML pages + shared vanilla JS render modules
Every project/site field driven by one JSON record
No build step, no framework, no bundler

groups.label: Software
items: Category filter bar on the Projects page
Modular case-study system (this section is one such module)
Print-ready CV page generated from its own JSON

items.label: Challenges
items.text: Balancing ambient visual effects (canvas backgrounds, cursor, tilt) against real performance, several rounds of profiling were needed to remove jank without losing the premium feel.

items.label: Future Improvements
items.text: Add a lightweight build step for image optimization, and expand the modular project-content system with real photo galleries as projects gain documentation.

title: Formula Water
subtitle: Gravity-powered vehicle prototype
description: An engineering project focused on the design, modeling, and validation of a gravity-powered Formula Water prototype. The repository includes CAD development, engineering calculations, analytical modeling, numerical simulations, and prototype iterations used to optimize performance and efficiency. The project combines mechanical design, applied physics, manufacturing considerations, and experimental validation to demonstrate a structured engineering workflow from concept development through testing and technical documentation.
objectives: Design a vehicle that converts the potential energy of falling water into forward motion as efficiently as possible.
Minimize friction and mass losses across the drivetrain to maximize distance travelled per unit of stored energy.
Validate the design analytically and experimentally before the competition run.
outcome: 1st place at the University of Minho competition, with a measured run distance of 21 m against a 22.5 m theoretical prediction. The ~6.7% shortfall was traced back to added friction in the 3D-printed drivetrain components, giving an overall energy-conversion efficiency of about 14.1%.

story.text: The brief was to design a vehicle powered solely by the potential energy of a falling water mass, maximizing distance travelled, a problem that lives at the intersection of energy conversion, drivetrain efficiency, and mass/friction management.

The team studied energy-conversion mechanisms (falling-mass-driven spools, gear trains) and prior competition designs to identify where energy is typically lost, mainly friction in bearings and inefficient torque transfer at low speeds.

I worked on the CAD models in SolidWorks and Solid Edge for the chassis and drivetrain components, focusing on a lightweight structure with a gear ratio tuned to keep the falling mass near its optimal descent speed throughout the run.

Used Python to model the system's dynamics, energy conversion, drivetrain losses, rolling friction, and stability/center-of-mass behavior, iterating the design parameters against the simulation before committing to physical builds.
Translated the CAD models into manufactured components, assembling the drivetrain and chassis and iterating on tolerances and bearing selection to reduce friction losses identified in simulation.

Ran physical trials to validate the simulated performance, measuring an actual run distance of 21 m versus the 22.5 m predicted analytically, then made small adjustments to gear ratio and mass distribution based on the ~6.7% shortfall observed.

The prototype won 1st place at the University of Minho competition. Measured performance did not fully match the model: the vehicle covered 21 m against a theoretical prediction of 22.5 m, an overall efficiency of roughly 14.1%. The gap was traced to extra friction from the 3D-printed drivetrain parts that the idealized Python model hadn't fully captured. That honest theory-vs-measurement comparison, rather than a perfect match, is what confirmed the analytical approach.
Simulating the system in Python before committing to manufacturing saved iteration cycles, most of the physical testing was spent fine-tuning rather than discovering fundamental design flaws.

title: Door Lock Teardown
subtitle: Reverse-engineering an automotive mechanism
description: A comprehensive engineering teardown of an automotive door lock mechanism involving complete disassembly, reverse engineering, CAD reconstruction, and functional analysis. The project investigates component interactions, manufacturing processes, material selection, tolerances, and assembly methods to understand the system's operation and design intent. The resulting documentation highlights both the mechanical architecture and engineering decisions behind a real automotive product.
objectives: Fully disassemble an automotive door lock mechanism to understand every component's function.
Identify the materials and manufacturing processes behind each part and why they were chosen.
Document the mechanism well enough to explain the engineering decisions behind the design.
outcome: A complete component-by-component breakdown of the mechanism, with documented reasoning for material and process choices and how each part contributes to the lock's function and reliability.

story.text: Consumer and automotive products are full of small mechanisms whose design intent isn't obvious from the outside, I wanted to understand how a real door lock actually works and why it was built the way it was.
Before disassembly, I researched typical automotive lock mechanisms and common failure points to know what to look for once the parts were exposed.
Carefully disassembled the mechanism, cataloguing every component, its material, and its interaction with neighboring parts, springs, levers, the actuation linkage, and the locking pawl.
Manually cycled sub-assemblies after disassembly to confirm how forces travel through the mechanism and validate my understanding of the actuation sequence.

Produced a documented breakdown covering each component's material, manufacturing process (stamping, injection molding, machining), and its role in the overall mechanism, a clear map of the engineering decisions behind the product.

Reverse engineering a finished product is one of the fastest ways to build intuition for manufacturing-aware design, tolerances and material choices that look arbitrary on paper usually have a clear cost or reliability reason once you see the assembled part.

items.label: Future Improvements

title: Fatigue Study
subtitle: FEA-based fatigue life assessment of a transmission hub
description: A structural integrity study of a transmission hub in EN-GJS-500-7 nodular cast iron (σᵤ = 500 MPa, σᵧ = 320 MPa, E = 169 GPa), triggered by a real part that failed in service. Combines CAD modeling, Finite Element Analysis under a cyclic impact load (Fₘₐₓ = 12,000 N, Fₘᵢₙ = 3,000 N, R = 0.25), and analytical calculations to evaluate stress distribution and fatigue performance. A four-step mesh-convergence study confirmed the FEA result, and the resulting simulated and hand-calculated fatigue lives were compared against each other and against the real failure.
objectives: Model a transmission hub in CAD and evaluate its stress distribution under cyclic loading.
Identify stress-concentration regions most likely to initiate fatigue failure.
Cross-validate the FEA results against analytical solid-mechanics calculations.
outcome: A validated fatigue-life estimate for the hub: FEA (converged at a 1 mm mesh / 2.36M elements, 242 MPa peak von Mises stress) predicted failure around 94 impact cycles, while an analytical Goodman-criterion check (Kf = 2.3, safety factor 1.5) predicted around 1,000 cycles. Both methods agree on a finite, short fatigue life, consistent with the arm that actually broke in service.

story.text: This study started from a real failure: a transmission-hub arm broke in service under cyclic impact loading. Predicting where fatigue failure initiates, and how long the part will actually last, requires more than a static-stress check.
Reviewed fatigue theory (S-N curves, stress concentration factors, mean/alternating stress effects) to establish the correct approach for a component under cyclic, non-uniform loading.

Built a CAD model of the hub in EN-GJS-500-7 nodular cast iron, capturing the geometric features most likely to concentrate stress (fillets, keyways, and section transitions) under the measured cyclic impact load (Fₘₐₓ = 12,000 N, Fₘᵢₙ = 3,000 N, stress ratio R = 0.25).

Ran a mesh-convergence study across four refinement levels before trusting the FEA result, converging at a 1 mm mesh (2.36 million elements) with a peak von Mises stress of 242 MPa. Cross-checked that value against an analytical Goodman-criterion calculation (stress concentration Kf = 2.3, target safety factor 1.5) at the same critical section.

The converged FEA model (242 MPa peak stress) predicted roughly 94 impact cycles to failure; the analytical Goodman-criterion check predicted roughly 1,000 cycles. The two methods diverge in absolute count but agree on the conclusion that matters: a short, finite fatigue life at that stress concentration, consistent with the real arm that failed in service.

FEA results are only as trustworthy as the mesh and the analytical checks behind them. Running the four-step convergence study before reading the stress value, and cross-checking with Goodman by hand, is what made the ~94 vs ~1,000-cycle gap interpretable instead of just a red flag.

title: Pin Clutch
subtitle: Pedal-actuated pin clutch mechanism
description: Design and development of a pedal-actuated pin clutch mechanism (a coupling system in the same family used on sewing machines) intended for controlled shaft engagement and disengagement. The driving pulley carries three concentric grooves; a spring-loaded radial pin slides into one of them to lock the pulley to a driven shaft, and a pedal-actuated lever compresses the spring to withdraw the pin on demand. The project includes concept generation, CAD modeling in Solid Edge, a full kinematic analysis (position, velocity, and acceleration of the engagement point via rotation-matrix formulation), material selection, and functional prototyping using additive manufacturing. Particular attention was given to simplicity, manufacturability, and reliable operation, demonstrating the complete engineering design process from initial concept to a validated physical prototype.
objectives: Design a simple, reliable mechanism to engage and disengage two shafts on demand via a pedal, using a three-groove driving pulley and a spring-loaded radial pin.
Keep the design manufacturable with additive manufacturing (FDM/PLA) and low-cost secondary materials (pine wood, PVC, carbon-steel spring wire).
Derive the full kinematic model (position, velocity, and acceleration) of the engagement point to validate the linkage geometry analytically.
outcome: A working PLA prototype that reliably engages and disengages two shafts via pedal actuation and a spring-loaded pin, with the kinematic model (position, velocity, and acceleration of the pin's engagement point, derived through rotation-matrix transformations) confirming the linkage geometry chosen in CAD.

story.text: The goal was a mechanism that lets an operator engage or disengage two rotating shafts on demand, using a simple pedal input rather than a complex clutch assembly.

Looked at simple mechanical clutch principles, pin/dog clutches in particular, tracing the lineage from medieval leather-belt mill couplings through Industrial Revolution line-shaft pulleys, cone clutches, and modern dry disc and dual-clutch (PDK/DSG) systems, for a design that trades some smoothness for mechanical simplicity and manufacturability.

Designed a pin-based engagement system around a driving pulley with three concentric grooves: pressing the pedal releases a curved lever that was holding the radial pin retracted against a compressed spring, letting the pin snap into a groove and lock the pulley to the driven shaft; releasing the pedal lets the lever push the pin back out, decoupling the shafts.

Modeled the mechanism in Solid Edge and ran a full kinematic analysis of the pin's engagement point: position from a rotation-matrix transform of the local frame (r = A₁·s), velocity from w₁/₀ ∧ s₁^A, and acceleration from w₁/₀(w₁/₀ ∧ s₁^A) under constant angular velocity, sizing the actuation travel and confirming reliable engagement across the expected range of motion.
3D-printed the components in PLA, choosing print orientation and tolerances to keep the pin sliding smoothly in its housing without excessive play.
Cycled the prototype by hand to confirm repeatable engagement and disengagement, adjusting clearances where friction or misalignment caused inconsistent locking.

A functional, low-cost prototype that consistently demonstrates the coupling/decoupling principle, with the analytical kinematic model matching the CAD linkage geometry and validating the pedal-actuated pin-clutch concept end to end.
Even a small mechanism benefits from a real kinematic pass before printing, an early paper sketch of the linkage geometry would have caught a clearance issue I only found after the first print.

items.label: Challenges
items.text: Getting the pin-to-groove clearance right (too tight caused binding, too loose caused inconsistent engagement), and correctly modeling the impact-like tangential force that briefly decelerates the pulley at the moment of engagement.

items.text: Sketch and size the linkage geometry on paper before the first CAD pass, and instrument the prototype to measure the pulley's momentary speed drop at engagement predicted by the kinematic model.
